claim: Nicotinic partial agonists provide an accepted aid for smoking cessation and contribute to decreasing tobacco-related disease.
source: Nicotinic partial agonists provide an accepted aid for smoking cessation and thus contribute to decreasing tobacco-related disease.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical practice and consensus in the field.

claim: There is no reductionist method to examine the cellular and subcellular pharmacokinetic properties of nicotinic partial agonists in living cells.
source: However, there remains no reductionist method to examine the cellular and subcellular pharmacokinetic properties of these compounds in living cells.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current methodology that the study aims to address.

claim: New intensity-based drug-sensing fluorescent reporters (iDrugSnFRs) were developed for dianicline, cytisine, 10-fluorocytisine, and 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine.
source: Here, we developed new intensity-based drug-sensing fluorescent reporters (iDrugSnFRs) for the nicotinic partial agonists dianicline, cytisine, and two cytisine derivatives – 10-fluorocytisine and 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine.
evidence: This is the primary experimental contribution described in the abstract.

claim: The first atomic-scale structures of liganded periplasmic binding protein-based biosensors were reported.
source: We report the first atomic-scale structures of liganded periplasmic binding protein-based biosensors, accelerating development of iDrugSnFRs and also explaining the activation mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystallographic data presented in the manuscript (PDB entries 7S7U, 7S7T, 7S7V).

claim: The nicotinic iDrugSnFRs detect their drug partners in solution, at the plasma membrane, and in the endoplasmic reticulum of cell lines and mouse hippocampal neurons.
source: The nicotinic iDrugSnFRs detect their drug partners in solution, as well as at the plasma membrane (PM) and in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of cell lines and mouse hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: At the plasma membrane, the speed of solution changes limits the growth and decay rates of the fluorescence response in almost all cases.
source: At the PM, the speed of solution changes limits the growth and decay rates of the fluorescence response in almost all cases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of kinetic data from cellular experiments.

claim: Rates of membrane crossing differ among nicotinic drugs by more than 30-fold.
source: In contrast, we found that rates of membrane crossing differ among these nicotinic drugs by >30-fold.
evidence: This is a quantitative conclusion from the cellular imaging experiments comparing different drugs.

claim: Partial agonists with lower efficacy than nicotine could serve as effective smoking-cessation drugs.
source: Prior work suggests that partial agonists with lower efficacy than nicotine could serve as effective smoking-cessation drugs (Rose et al., 1994), and efforts continue in that direction (Rollema and Hurst, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cytisine is an α4β2 nAChR partial agonist.
source: Another plant alkaloid, (-)-cytisine (also called cytisinicline and Tabex), an α4β2 nAChR partial agonist, served as a basis for the synthesis of analogs that have not yet entered the clinic (Chellappan et al., 2006; Houllier et al., 2006; Imming et al., 2001; Kozikowski et al., 2007; Marcaurelle et al., 2009; Philipova et al., 2015; Rouden et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a pharmacological characterization supported by citations.

claim: Varenicline is currently the only FDA-approved smoking-cessation drug.
source: Varenicline (Chantix) has four rings, two more than nicotine or cytisine, and is currently the only FDA-approved smoking-cessation drug, but the modest quit rate of ~18% at 12 months invites further investigation (Coe et al., 2005; Mills et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory approval status supported by citations.

claim: Varenicline has a quit rate of approximately 18% at 12 months.
source: Varenicline (Chantix) has four rings, two more than nicotine or cytisine, and is currently the only FDA-approved smoking-cessation drug, but the modest quit rate of ~18% at 12 months invites further investigation (Coe et al., 2005; Mills et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a clinical outcome statistic supported by citations.

claim: Dianicline was discontinued after unfavorable Phase III clinical trials.
source: Dianicline, another tetracyclic compound, was discontinued after unfavorable Phase III clinical trials (Cohen et al., 2003; Fagerstrom and Balfour, 2006).
evidence: This is a historical fact about drug development supported by citations.

claim: A nicotinic ligand for smoking cessation must enter the brain where the most nicotine-sensitive nAChRs (α4β2) occur.
source: A nicotinic ligand for smoking cessation must satisfy at least three criteria (Rollema et al., 2010; Tashkin, 2015). (1) It must enter the brain, where the most nicotine-sensitive nAChRs (α4β2) occur.
evidence: This is a criterion for drug development supported by citations.

claim: A nicotinic ligand for smoking cessation must activate α4β2 nAChRs with an EC50 sufficient to reduce cravings and withdrawal (1–2 μM).
source: It must also (2) activate α4β2 nAChRs with an EC50 sufficient to reduce cravings and withdrawal (1–2 μM).
evidence: This is a pharmacological criterion for drug development.

claim: A nicotinic ligand for smoking cessation must block nicotine binding to reduce the reward phase of smoking (2–30 min).
source: Finally, it must (3) block nicotine binding to reduce the reward phase of smoking (2–30 min).
evidence: This is a pharmacological criterion for drug development.

claim: Varenicline meets the three criteria for a smoking-cessation drug.
source: Varenicline meets these criteria, while cytisine (low brain penetration) and dianicline (EC50 = 18 μM) each fail one of the criteria (Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative evaluation supported by citation.

claim: Cytisine has low brain penetration.
source: Varenicline meets these criteria, while cytisine (low brain penetration) and dianicline (EC50 = 18 μM) each fail one of the criteria (Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a pharmacokinetic property supported by citation.

claim: Dianicline has an EC50 of 18 μM.
source: Varenicline meets these criteria, while cytisine (low brain penetration) and dianicline (EC50 = 18 μM) each fail one of the criteria (Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a pharmacological measurement supported by citation.

claim: For uncharged molecules, the conventional metric for membrane permeability is logP, where P is the octanol-water partition coefficient.
source: For uncharged molecules, the conventional metric for membrane permeability is logP, where P is the octanol-water partition coefficient.
evidence: This is established knowledge in pharmacology and chemistry.

claim: For weak bases, logP must be corrected to account for the fraction of uncharged molecules at pH 7.4, resulting in logDpH7.4.
source: For weak bases including most orally available neural drugs, logP must be corrected to account for the fraction of uncharged (deprotonated) molecules at the pH of interest, usually pH 7.4; the resulting metric, termed logDpH7.4, is always less positive than logP.
evidence: This is established knowledge in pharmacology.

claim: 10-fluorocytisine and 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine have cytisine-like EC50 for α4β2 nAChRs.
source: Two of the resulting derivatives, 10-fluorocytisine and 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine, have cytisine-like EC50 for the α4β2 nAChRs, but more positive calculated logDpH7.4 values, suggesting greater membrane permeability at the nearly neutral pH of the blood, brain, and cytoplasm (Blom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a pharmacological characterization supported by citation.

claim: 10-fluorocytisine and 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine have more positive calculated logDpH7.4 values than cytisine, suggesting greater membrane permeability.
source: Two of the resulting derivatives, 10-fluorocytisine and 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine, have cytisine-like EC50 for the α4β2 nAChRs, but more positive calculated logDpH7.4 values, suggesting greater membrane permeability at the nearly neutral pH of the blood, brain, and cytoplasm (Blom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a computational prediction and inference about membrane permeability supported by citation.

claim: Estimates of logDpH7.4 are inexact and differ over 2 log units for individual molecules depending on the algorithm used.
source: Estimates of logDpH7.4 are inexact, extrapolated, or rely on algorithmic calculations whose results differ over 2 log units for individual molecules (Pieńko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a limitation of computational methods supported by citation.

claim: Nicotine enters the endoplasmic reticulum, binds to nascent nAChRs, and causes selective upregulation of these receptors on the plasma membrane.
source: Nicotine itself (logDpH7.4 0.99) enters the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), binds to nascent nAChRs, becomes a pharmacological chaperone for the nAChRs, and eventually causes selective upregulation of these receptors on the plasma membrane (PM) (Henderson and Lester, 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of nicotine's effects supported by citation.

claim: Nicotine has a logDpH7.4 of 0.99.
source: Nicotine itself (logDpH7.4 0.99) enters the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), binds to nascent nAChRs, becomes a pharmacological chaperone for the nAChRs, and eventually causes selective upregulation of these receptors on the plasma membrane (PM) (Henderson and Lester, 2015).
evidence: This is a calculated physicochemical property.

claim: Nicotine and varenicline enter the ER within seconds of drug application and exit equally rapidly upon extracellular washing.
source: We previously explored the subcellular pharmacokinetics of nicotine and varenicline in immortalized cell lines and cultured neurons using the iDrugSnFRs iNicSnFR3a and iNicSnFR3b to visualize that these nicotinic agonists enter the ER within seconds of drug application and exit equally rapidly from the ER upon extracellular washing (Shivange et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Nicotine crosses six plasma membranes to enter the brain within 20 seconds.
source: That nicotine diffuses across cellular membranes in seconds has been suspected for decades: nicotine crosses six PMs to enter the brain within 20 s, providing a 'buzz.'
evidence: This is established knowledge about nicotine pharmacokinetics.

claim: Varenicline becomes trapped in acidic vesicles.
source: That varenicline becomes trapped in acidic vesicles suggests appreciable membrane permeation but may also underlie unwanted effects (Govind et al., 2017; Le Houezec, 2003).
evidence: This is a finding about varenicline's subcellular distribution supported by citations.

claim: Crystals of iNicSnFR3adt in the presence of 10 mM nicotine diffracted to 2.95 Å resolution.
source: Crystals of iNicSnFR3adt in the presence of 10 mM nicotine diffracted to 2.95 Å resolution (PDB 7S7U).
evidence: This is a crystallographic result from the study.

claim: The liganded periplasmic binding protein domain of iNicSnFR3adt adopts a closed conformation.
source: Overall, the liganded periplasmic binding protein (PBP) domain of iNicSnFR3adt adopts a closed conformation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallography shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Crystals of iNicSnFR3adt with varenicline bound diffracted to 3.2 Å resolution.
source: Crystals of iNicSnFR3adt with varenicline bound were isomorphous to those of the nicotine-bound crystals and diffracted to 3.2 Å resolution (PDB 7S7T).
evidence: This is a crystallographic result from the study.

claim: Varenicline forms cation-π interactions with Tyr65 and Tyr357 in the iNicSnFR3adt binding pocket.
source: Varenicline is enclosed by the same aromatic residues as nicotine, forming cation-π interactions with Tyr65 and Tyr357, in addition to other interactions with the pocket residues (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallography shown in Figure 1.

claim: Similar ligand-induced conformational changes occur in the PBP for nicotine, varenicline, ACh, and choline.
source: The data confirm that similar ligand-induced conformational changes occur in the PBP for nicotine, varenicline, ACh (Borden et al., 2019), and choline (Fan, 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis supported by citations and figure supplement.

claim: In the apo state, Glu78 in Linker 1 approaches within approximately 2.5 Å of the oxygen of the tyrosine fluorophore.
source: In the full iDrugSnFR, in the apo state, the Glu78 in Linker 1 approaches within ~2.5 Å of the oxygen of the tyrosine fluorophore (Figure 1E1; PDB 7S7V).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallography shown in Figure 1E1.

claim: In the liganded state, Glu78 has moved away from the fluorophore, presumably allowing the fluorescent tyrosinate to form.
source: Figure 1E2 provides structural details confirming the hypothesis (Barnett et al., 2017; Nasu et al., 2021) that in the liganded state Glu78 has moved away, presumably allowing the fluorescent tyrosinate to form (Video 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation and mechanistic interpretation supported by citations and shown in Figure 1E2.

claim: The mechanism by which Glu78 prevents fluorescence in the apo state is termed the 'candle snuffer' mechanism.
source: We term this mechanism the 'candle snuffer'.
evidence: This is a descriptive term coined by the authors for the mechanism.

claim: iDianiSnFR has an EC50 of 6.7 ± 0.3 µM, ΔFmax/F0 of 7.4 ± 0.1, and S-slope of 1.1.
source: The dianicline sensor, iDianiSnFR, has EC50 6.7 ± 0.3 µM, ΔFmax/F0 7.4 ± 0.1, and S-slope 1.1.
evidence: These are measured parameters from dose-response experiments shown in Table 1 and Figure 2A.

claim: iCytSnFR has an EC50 of 9.4 ± 0.8 µM, ΔFmax/F0 of 5.0 ± 0.2, and S-slope of 0.5.
source: The cytisine sensor, iCytSnFR, has EC50 9.4 ± 0.8 µM, ΔFmax/F0 5.0 ± 0.2, and S-slope 0.5 (Table 1, Figure 2A and B).
evidence: These are measured parameters from dose-response experiments shown in Table 1 and Figure 2B.

claim: iCyt_F_SnFR has an EC50 of 1.4 ± 0.04 µM, ΔFmax/F0 of 7.9 ± 0.1, and S-slope of 5.6.
source: This optimization gave us iCyt_F_SnFR (EC50 1.4 ± 0.04 µM, ΔFmax/F0 7.9 ± 0.1, S-slope 5.6) and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR (EC50 5.7 ± 0.1 µM, ΔFmax/F0 4.0 ± 0.03, and S-slope 0.7) (Table 1, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: These are measured parameters from dose-response experiments shown in Table 1 and Figure 2C.

claim: iCyt_BrEt_SnFR has an EC50 of 5.7 ± 0.1 µM, ΔFmax/F0 of 4.0 ± 0.03, and S-slope of 0.7.
source: This optimization gave us iCyt_F_SnFR (EC50 1.4 ± 0.04 µM, ΔFmax/F0 7.9 ± 0.1, S-slope 5.6) and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR (EC50 5.7 ± 0.1 µM, ΔFmax/F0 4.0 ± 0.03, and S-slope 0.7) (Table 1, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: These are measured parameters from dose-response experiments shown in Table 1 and Figure 2D.

claim: The newly developed iDrugSnFRs showed some sensitivity to related nicotinic agonists.
source: The newly developed iDrugSnFRs showed some sensitivity to related nicotinic agonists.
evidence: This is a summary of specificity testing results shown in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: iDianiSnFR had the greatest fidelity for its drug partner among the newly developed sensors.
source: iDianiSnFR had the greatest fidelity for its drug partner but also showed an increased EC50 (15 µM) as a purified protein versus its EC50 in lysate (6.7 µM), possibly indicating decreased stability in a purified form.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment based on specificity data in Table 2 and Figure 3A.

claim: iCytSnFR, iCyt_F_SnFR, and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR have an exceptionally low (60-90 nM) EC50 for varenicline.
source: Of note, iCytSnFR, iCyt_F_SnFR, and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR have an exceptionally low (60‒90 nM) EC50 for varenicline.
evidence: This is a measured parameter from dose-response experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: The newly developed iDrugSnFRs showed negligible binding to choline or acetylcholine.
source: The newly developed iDrugSnFRs showed negligible binding to choline or the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, leading one to expect minimal endogenous interference during future in vivo experiments.
evidence: This is a specificity result from dose-response experiments shown in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: iDianiSnFR showed no fluorescent response to any of the selected endogenous molecules.
source: iDianiSnFR showed no response to any of the nine selected compounds above background.
evidence: This is a specificity result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: iCytSnFR, iCyt_F_SnFR, and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR exhibited a ΔF/F0 of 0.25-0.8 to dopamine at 316 µM/1 mM.
source: However, they exhibited a ΔF/F0 of 0.25‒0.8 to dopamine at 316 µM/1 mM and a ΔF/F0 of 0.8–1.5 to serotonin (5-HT) at 316 µM/1 mM.
evidence: This is a specificity result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: iCytSnFR, iCyt_F_SnFR, and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR exhibited a ΔF/F0 of 0.8-1.5 to serotonin at 316 µM/1 mM.
source: However, they exhibited a ΔF/F0 of 0.25‒0.8 to dopamine at 316 µM/1 mM and a ΔF/F0 of 0.8–1.5 to serotonin (5-HT) at 316 µM/1 mM.
evidence: This is a specificity result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SnFRs are at least 250-fold more sensitive to their eponymous partners than to other molecules tested.
source: In terms of S-slope, the relevant metric for most cellular or in vivo experiments, the SnFRs are at least 250-fold more sensitive to their eponymous partners than to other molecules we have tested.
evidence: This is a calculated selectivity metric based on S-slope comparisons.

claim: The experimentally determined KD of each iDrugSnFR:drug pair using ITC was within a factor of 1.5 from the experimentally determined EC50 for fluorescence.
source: The experimentally determined KD of each iDrugSnFR:drug pair using ITC was within a factor of 1.5 from the experimentally determined EC50 for fluorescence in E. coli lysate or purified protein (Table 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of thermodynamic measurements shown in Table 3 and Figure 4.

claim: The EC50 for fluorescence is dominated by the overall binding of the ligand for all the iDrugSnFRs.
source: We infer that the EC50 for fluorescence is dominated by the overall binding of the ligand for all the iDrugSnFRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the agreement between KD and EC50 values.

claim: The heats for iCytSnFR, iCyt_F_SnFR, and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR binding were exothermic.
source: The heats for iCytSnFR, iCyt_F_SnFR, and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR were exothermic, while that for iDianiSnFR was endothermic.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic observation from ITC experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The heat for iDianiSnFR binding was endothermic.
source: The heats for iCytSnFR, iCyt_F_SnFR, and iCyt_BrEt_SnFR were exothermic, while that for iDianiSnFR was endothermic.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic observation from ITC experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: All iDrugSnFRs show exergonic reactions.
source: All iDrugSnFRs show exergonic reactions, but the relative enthalpic and entropic contributions vary among iDrugSnFRs.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic conclusion from ITC data shown in Figure 4 and Table 3.

claim: iDrugSnFRs do not have pseudo-first-order kinetic behaviors typical of two-state binding interactions.
source: The stopped-flow data revealed that iDrugSnFRs do not have pseudo-first-order kinetic behaviors typical of two-state binding interactions.
evidence: This is a kinetic observation from stopped-flow experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Most of the fluorescence change for iDianiSnFR occurs within the first 0.1 s of mixing.
source: Most of the fluorescence change occurs within the first 0.1 s of mixing (Figure 5A), with only minor additional increase by 100 s.
evidence: This is a kinetic observation from stopped-flow experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The decay of the ACh response followed a single exponential time course with a time constant τoff of 530 ± 30 ms.
source: Decay of the ACh response followed a single exponential time course (Figure 6B). The values of the koff for 30, 100, and 200 µM ACh did not differ significantly (ANOVA, p=0.62, degrees of freedom [df] = 2 (model), 20 [error]). We pooled them to obtain a mean koff of 1.9 ± 0.1 s–1 (mean ± SEM, n = 23 areas [50 cells]). The corresponding time constant τ0ff was 530 ± 30 ms.
evidence: This is a kinetic measurement from microperfusion experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The temporal resolution of the CytSnFR_PM sensor for changes in ACh concentration is in the subsecond range.
source: Hence, the temporal resolution of the CytSnFR_PM sensor for changes in the ACh concentration was in the subsecond range.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured decay kinetics.

claim: The decay of the cytisine response was biphasic with time constants of 1.8 ± 0.1 s and 6.9 ± 0.2 s.
source: The kfoff and ksoff for 5–15 µM cytisine were 0.61 ± 0.04 s–1 (n = 36 areas, 105 cells) and 0.146 ± 0.006 s–1 (n = 35 areas, n = 103 cells), respectively. The corresponding decay time constants (τf0ff, τs0ff) were 1.8 ± 0.1 s and 6.9 ± 0.2 s.
evidence: This is a kinetic measurement from microperfusion experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The temporal resolution of CytSnFR_PM sensor for cytisine is less than 10 s.
source: Therefore, the temporal resolution of CytSnFR_PM sensor for cytisine was <10 s, adequate for the temporal resolution of the live-cell experiments presented below.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured decay kinetics.

claim: The decay waveform of the varenicline response was much slower than that for cytisine or ACh.
source: Interestingly, the decay waveform of the varenicline response was much slower than that for cytisine or ACh (Figure 6A and D).
evidence: This is a comparative kinetic observation from microperfusion experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The temporal resolution of the iCytSnFR_PM sensor for varenicline is in the minute range.
source: Thus, the temporal resolution of the iCytSnFR_PM sensor for varenicline was in the minute range.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured decay kinetics for varenicline.

claim: iDianiSnFR showed a robust response to dianicline at the PM and ER in HeLa cells across a range of concentrations (3.125-100 µM).
source: iDianiSnFR showed a robust response to dianicline at the PM and the ER in HeLa cells across a range of concentrations (3.125‒100 µM), and the speed was nearly limited by solution exchanges; there was a clear return to baseline fluorescence upon washout on the order of seconds after each drug application.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At 100 µM dianicline, the PM and ER have a ΔF/F0 of approximately 1.2.
source: At 100 µM, the PM and ER have a ΔF/F0 of ~1.2, but at lower concentrations, the ER displayed 30–75% of the signal detected at the PM, which may indicate a difference in membrane crossing (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At lower dianicline concentrations, the ER displayed 30-75% of the signal detected at the PM.
source: At 100 µM, the PM and ER have a ΔF/F0 of ~1.2, but at lower concentrations, the ER displayed 30–75% of the signal detected at the PM, which may indicate a difference in membrane crossing (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from live-cell imaging shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cytisine showed slower entry into and exit from the ER of HeLa cells compared to the PM.
source: Cytisine showed slower entry into and exit from the ER of HeLa cells.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The iCytSnFR_PM construct detected cytisine at concentrations from 0.078 to 80 µM with a return to baseline fluorescence upon washout on the order of seconds.
source: The iCytSnFR_PM construct detected cytisine at concentrations from 0.078 to 80 µM and demonstrated a return to baseline fluorescence upon washout on the order of seconds after each drug application, reaching a maximum ΔF/F0 of ~2 at concentrations above 5 µM (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The iCytSnFR_ER construct only detected cytisine with a ΔF/F0 above the buffer control in the range of 1.25 to 80 µM.
source: In contrast to the _PM construct, the iCytSnFR_ER construct only detected cytisine with a ΔF/F0 above the buffer control in the range of concentrations from 1.25 to 80 µM with a ΔF/F0, which was 25–50% of the maximum ΔF/F0 detected at the PM.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The washout of cytisine from the ER was much slower than solution changes.
source: Additionally, in the range of detectable concentrations of cytisine, the washout of cytisine was much slower than solution changes (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Cytisine and 10-fluorocytisine require washout times of several minutes from the ER even when applied at concentrations as low as 0.1 µM and 0.316 µM.
source: However, it is noteworthy that even when applied at concentrations as low as 0.1 µM and 0.316 µM, cytisine and 10-fluorocytisine require washout times of several minutes from the ER.
evidence: This is an observation from extended washout experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: iCytSnFR and iCyt_F_SnFR both bind nicotine in the same concentration range as cytisine.
source: iCytSnFR and iCyt_F_SnFR both bind nicotine in the same concentration range as cytisine (though with lower ΔF/F0).
evidence: This is a specificity observation from dose-response experiments.

claim: Nicotine waveforms with iCytSnFR_ER and iCyt_F_SnFR_ER resembled those published with iNicSnFR3a and iNicSnFR3b.
source: These nicotine waveforms resembled those already published with iNicSnFR3a and iNicSnFR3b (Shivange et al., 2019), confirming that iCytSnFR_ER functions as expected with a more permeant nicotinic drug.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from control experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2, supported by citation.

claim: The slower kinetics for iCytSnFR_ER with cytisine and iCyt_F_SnFR_ER with 10-fluorocytisine arise because these drugs cross membranes more slowly.
source: Thus, the slower kinetics for iCytSnFR_ER with cytisine and iCyt_F_SnFR_ER with 10-fluorocytisine arise because these drugs cross membranes more slowly.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing nicotine and cytisine/10-fluorocytisine kinetics with the same sensors.

claim: Cytisine and 10-fluorocytisine cross the membrane more than 30-fold more slowly than the other drugs tested.
source: We restrict the quantitative comparisons to the estimate that cytisine and 10-fluorocytisine cross the membrane >30-fold more slowly than the other drugs tested.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on comparing kinetics across different drugs in cellular experiments.

claim: This study shows the first time-resolved measurements of membrane permeation for drugs in the logDpH7.4 range less than -1.
source: The experiments show, to our knowledge, the first time-resolved measurements of membrane permeation for drugs in the logDpH7.4 range less than –1.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach.

claim: Most orally available drugs have logDpH7.4 values between 2 and 4.
source: Most orally available drugs have logDpH7.4 values between 2 and 4 (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge in pharmaceutical science supported by citation.

claim: Cytisine, varenicline, dianicline, and the cytisine analogs have calculated membrane partition coefficients 3-6 orders of magnitude lower than most orally available drugs.
source: Cytisine, varenicline, dianicline, and the cytisine analogs studied here have calculated membrane partition coefficients some 3–6 orders of magnitude lower.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about physicochemical properties.

claim: 10-fluorocytisine has a calculated logDpH7.4 of -2.70.
source: here, we provide values calculated by Chemicalize (see Materials and methods): 10-fluorocytisine, –2.70; cytisine, –2.64; dianicline, –1.29; varenicline, –1.27; 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine, –1.13.
evidence: This is a calculated physicochemical property.

claim: Cytisine has a calculated logDpH7.4 of -2.64.
source: here, we provide values calculated by Chemicalize (see Materials and methods): 10-fluorocytisine, –2.70; cytisine, –2.64; dianicline, –1.29; varenicline, –1.27; 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine, –1.13.
evidence: This is a calculated physicochemical property.

claim: Dianicline has a calculated logDpH7.4 of -1.29.
source: here, we provide values calculated by Chemicalize (see Materials and methods): 10-fluorocytisine, –2.70; cytisine, –2.64; dianicline, –1.29; varenicline, –1.27; 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine, –1.13.
evidence: This is a calculated physicochemical property.

claim: Varenicline has a calculated logDpH7.4 of -1.27.
source: here, we provide values calculated by Chemicalize (see Materials and methods): 10-fluorocytisine, –2.70; cytisine, –2.64; dianicline, –1.29; varenicline, –1.27; 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine, –1.13.
evidence: This is a calculated physicochemical property.

claim: 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine has a calculated logDpH7.4 of -1.13.
source: here, we provide values calculated by Chemicalize (see Materials and methods): 10-fluorocytisine, –2.70; cytisine, –2.64; dianicline, –1.29; varenicline, –1.27; 9-bromo-10-ethylcytisine, –1.13.
evidence: This is a calculated physicochemical property.

claim: Drugs with logDpH7.4 values less than approximately -2 cross membranes much more slowly than ligands with logDpH7.4 greater than approximately -2.
source: Our measurements show that nicotinic ligands with logDpH7.4 < ~–2 cross membranes much more slowly than do ligands with logDpH7.4 > ~–2.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the membrane permeation experiments.

claim: The calculated logDpH7.4 values fall in the same two classes as the measured kinetics of membrane permeability: 10-fluorocytisine and cytisine are the slowest, and only these two agonists have logDpH7.4 values less than -2.
source: According to some (but not all) algorithms, the calculated logDpH7.4 values fall in the same two classes as the measured kinetics of membrane permeability: 10-fluorocytisine and cytisine are the slowest, and only these two agonists have logDpH7.4 values < –2.
evidence: This is a correlation between calculated properties and measured kinetics.

claim: Differences among chemical properties of nicotinic partial agonists correlate with drug permeation into the cerebrospinal fluid after peripheral administration in mice.
source: These observations support previous work suggesting that differences among chemical properties of nicotinic partial agonists correlate with drug permeation into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) after peripheral administration in mice (Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement connecting the current findings to prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The iDrugSnFRs are sensitive enough to allow experiments near the experimentally determined or projected concentration in human blood and CSF.
source: The iDrugSnFRs are sensitive enough to allow experiments near the experimentally determined (or otherwise projected) concentration in the human blood and CSF (Astroug et al., 2010; Jeong et al., 2018; Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the practical utility of the sensors, supported by citations.

claim: The iDrugSnFRs measure free aqueous ligand concentration ('activity'), as sensed by nAChRs.
source: The iDrugSnFRs have the advantage that they measure free aqueous ligand concentration ('activity'), as sensed by nAChRs.
evidence: This is a description of what the sensors measure.

claim: The experiments do not use radiolabeled drugs, in vivo microdialysis, experiments on live animals, or mass spectrometry-liquid chromatography instruments.
source: The experiments do not use radiolabeled drugs, in vivo microdialysis or other experiments on live animals, or mass spectrometry-liquid chromatography instruments.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological advantages of the approach.

claim: The candle snuffer mechanism explains several details of the agonist- and pH sensitivity of both iNicSnFR3a and iSketSnFR.
source: Because the candle snuffer mechanism explains several details of the agonist- and pH sensitivity of both iNicSnFR3a and iSketSnFR (see 'Discussion'), we presume that it represents a general mechanism for OpuBC-cpGFP SnFRs.
evidence: This is an inference about the generality of the mechanism based on its explanatory power.

claim: The candle snuffer mechanism represents a general mechanism for OpuBC-cpGFP SnFRs.
source: Because the candle snuffer mechanism explains several details of the agonist- and pH sensitivity of both iNicSnFR3a and iSketSnFR (see 'Discussion'), we presume that it represents a general mechanism for OpuBC-cpGFP SnFRs.
evidence: This is an inference about the generality of the mechanism.

claim: The apo form of the iDrugSnFR increases its F0 by 10-fold per pH unit.
source: (1) The apo form of the iDrugSnFR increases its F0 by 10-fold per pH unit (Shivange et al., 2019), as though when deprotonated, Glu78 leaves the 'candle snuffer' position and moves to make the salt bridges with Lys97 and Arg99.
evidence: This is a functional observation supporting the candle snuffer mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: The EC50 for the ligand decreases by 10-fold per pH unit.
source: (2) The EC50 for the ligand decreases by 10-fold per pH unit (Shivange et al., 2019), as though the conformation of the linker that forms the salt-bridge form is also the closed, liganded, fluorescent form of the PBP.
evidence: This is a functional observation supporting the candle snuffer mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: Only glutamate functions in position 78 of iSeroSnFR.
source: (3) Only glutamate functions in position 78 of iSeroSnFR (Unger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a mutagenesis result supporting the importance of Glu78, supported by citation.

claim: The mTurquoise variant in iGluSnFR, which has a tryptophan chromophore, requires entirely different linkers.
source: (4) The mTurquoise variant in iGluSnFR, which has a tryptophan chromophore, requires entirely different linkers (Marvin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation about chromophore-linker compatibility, supported by citation.

claim: α4β2 agonists that enter the ER, like nicotine and varenicline, upregulate nAChRs.
source: On the one hand, α4β2 agonists that enter the ER, like nicotine and varenicline, upregulate nAChRs (Turner et al., 2011), which may be necessary and sufficient for addiction (Henderson and Lester, 2015); and maintenance of upregulation by varenicline may help to explain its suboptimal quit rate.
evidence: This is a mechanistic statement about receptor upregulation supported by citations.

claim: Upregulation of nAChRs may be necessary and sufficient for addiction.
source: On the one hand, α4β2 agonists that enter the ER, like nicotine and varenicline, upregulate nAChRs (Turner et al., 2011), which may be necessary and sufficient for addiction (Henderson and Lester, 2015); and maintenance of upregulation by varenicline may help to explain its suboptimal quit rate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about addiction mechanisms supported by citation.

claim: Ligands that do not enter the ER are unlikely to enter the brain and therefore unlikely to be useful for smoking cessation.
source: On the other hand, ligands that do not enter the ER are also unlikely to enter the brain and therefore unlikely to be useful for smoking cessation.
evidence: This is a logical inference about drug development implications.

claim: Most drug metabolism takes place in the ER.
source: (1) Most drug metabolism takes place in the ER and (2) upregulation occurs at a sustained agonist concentration in the ER some hundredfold lower than the extracellular concentrations that transiently activate α4β2 nAChRs (Kuryatov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Upregulation occurs at a sustained agonist concentration in the ER some hundredfold lower than the extracellular concentrations that transiently activate α4β2 nAChRs.
source: (1) Most drug metabolism takes place in the ER and (2) upregulation occurs at a sustained agonist concentration in the ER some hundredfold lower than the extracellular concentrations that transiently activate α4β2 nAChRs (Kuryatov et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation about receptor upregulation supported by citation.

claim: The amine group of nicotinic ligands makes equidistant cation-π interactions with two tyrosine residues (Tyr65, Tyr357).
source: This study shows that the amine group of nicotinic ligands makes equidistant cation-π interactions with two tyrosine residues (Tyr65, Tyr357), and this is confirmed by higher-resolution (1.5–1.7 Å) structures of varenicline, acetylcholine, and choline crystallized with isolated PBP moieties (PDB 7S7X, SV1R, 7S7Z, respectively; see also 3R6U, 6EYQ, and 3PPQ).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallography.

claim: Cation-π interactions occur for cholinergic and/or nicotinic ligands in nAChRs, the acetylcholine-binding protein, PBPs, and muscarinic receptors.
source: Cation-π interactions also occur for cholinergic and/or nicotinic ligands in nAChRs (Morales-Perez et al., 2016; Post et al., 2017), the acetylcholine-binding protein (Celie et al., 2004), PBPs (Schiefner et al., 2004), and muscarinic receptors (Haga et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation across multiple protein families, supported by citations.

claim: The protonated amine of varenicline makes a hydrogen bond to a backbone carbonyl group.
source: We also observe that the protonated amine of varenicline makes a hydrogen bond to a backbone carbonyl group, another similar theme in acetylcholine binding protein (Celie et al., 2004) and nAChRs (Xiu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a structural observation from crystallography, supported by citations to similar interactions in other proteins.
